name: Australia
summary: Banks (authorised deposit-taking institutions) are prudentially supervised by APRA and conduct-regulated by ASIC, which jointly run the Financial Accountability Regime. AUSTRAC supervises AML/CTF; reformed rules in force since 31 March 2026 require AML/CTF policies to provide personnel due diligence and initial and ongoing training. The Australian Sanctions Office in DFAT administers sanctions, the OAIC enforces the Privacy Act, AFCA resolves complaints and the ATO receives FATCA/CRS reports. Most other duties are competence-based (licensee duties to train representatives, CPS 234, CPS 230, CPS 520) or come from the ASIC-approved Banking Code.

regulators.name: Australian Prudential Regulation Authority
regulators.role: Prudential regulator of banks: capital, governance, fit and proper, operational risk, information security, and co-regulator of FAR.

regulators.name: Australian Securities and Investments Commission
regulators.role: Conduct and licensing regulator for financial services and credit, including DDO, IDR, the Banking Code approval, FAR and the banking SPF code.

regulators.name: Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre
regulators.role: AML/CTF regulator and financial intelligence unit; administers the AML/CTF Act and Rules and receives SMRs and other reports.

regulators.name: Australian Sanctions Office (Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade)
regulators.role: Sanctions regulator under the Autonomous Sanctions Act 2011 and UN sanctions laws; maintains the Consolidated List and issues permits and guidance.

regulators.name: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
regulators.role: Privacy regulator under the Privacy Act 1988 (APPs and Notifiable Data Breaches scheme).

regulators.name: Australian Financial Complaints Authority
regulators.role: External dispute resolution scheme banks must join; will handle scam complaints under the SPF from 2027.

regulators.name: Australian Taxation Office
regulators.role: Receives FATCA and CRS reports from Australian financial institutions under the Taxation Administration Act 1953.

regulators.name: Australian Human Rights Commission
regulators.role: Enforces the positive duty to prevent sexual harassment under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984.

programs.title: Australia | AML/CTF Act 2006 and AML/CTF Rules 2025 Awareness
audience: All bank employees and contractors in AML/CTF roles
programs.why: Since 31 March 2026 a bank's AML/CTF policies must provide for due diligence on, and training of, staff who perform AML/CTF functions. AUSTRAC expects initial training on joining and ongoing refreshers tailored to each role's money laundering, terrorism financing and proliferation financing exposure, with completion records kept.

references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Section 26F(4)(d) (personnel due diligence) and 26F(4)(e) (personnel training)
references.note: As amended by the 2024 reforms, the AML/CTF policies must deal with due diligence on people who perform functions relevant to the entity's AML/CTF obligations (para (d)) and with training them on the ML/TF/PF risks the entity faces and on its obligations under the Act, regulations and Rules (para (e)).

references.title: Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Rules 2025
references.provision: Sections 5-8 (personnel due diligence) and 5-9 (providing personnel training)
references.note: Policies must cover initial training on joining and ongoing training during employment or engagement; training must suit the person's function, the ML/TF/PF risks of that function and their responsibilities under the policies, and be readily understandable.

references.title: AML/CTF training
references.note: AUSTRAC expects training to cover the entity's obligations and risks, to be tailored by role, refreshed often enough to keep pace with risk and legal change, and recorded.

programs.title: Australia | Training and Competence of AFS and Credit Representatives
audience: Staff providing financial product advice or dealing
programs.why: AFS licensees must ensure representatives are adequately trained and competent (Corporations Act s 912A(1)(f)), and credit licensees have the same duty (NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)). ASIC expects initial and ongoing training and supervision.

references.title: Corporations Act 2001
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Section 912A(1)(f)
references.note: AFS licensees must ensure their representatives are adequately trained (including through the CPD provisions where they apply) and competent to provide the licensed financial services.

references.title: National Consumer Credit Protection Act 2009
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Section 47(1)(g)
references.note: Credit licensees must ensure their representatives are adequately trained and competent to engage in the credit activities authorised by the licence.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 146 Licensing: Training of financial product advisers
references.note: Explains how licensees meet the duty to keep advisers trained and competent; advisers on basic deposit and related non-cash payment products can meet the standard through a course assessed by their licensee.

references.title: RG 105 AFS licensing: Organisational competence
references.note: Guidance on the licensee's organisational competence; it notes the separate duty to keep representatives trained and competent. ASIC expects an updated guide in the first quarter of 2027.

references.title: RG 206 Credit licensing: Competence and training
references.provision: NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)
references.note: Credit licensees must keep representatives adequately trained and competent (NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)); ASIC expects initial and ongoing training built into recruitment and supervision.

programs.title: Australia | Banking Code of Practice (2025) Compliance
programs.why: The ASIC-approved 2025 Banking Code commits subscribing banks to train staff to be competent and to understand the Code. It is an industry code binding through contract, not a statute.

references.title: Banking Code of Practice (2025)
references.provision: Clause 7 (trained and competent staff)
references.note: Industry code binding on subscribing banks; it commits banks to train staff to be competent, to know the Code and to deal with vulnerable customers with care.

references.title: 24-136MR ASIC approves enhanced Banking Code of Practice
references.note: ASIC approval of the 2025 Banking Code of Practice (from 28 February 2025), which broadens financial difficulty, improves accessibility and inclusion, and keeps the diligent and prudent banker standard; ASIC notes the Code binds ABA members through their customer contracts and that ASIC does not enforce it.

programs.title: Australia | Responsible Lending (NCCP Act and RG 209)
audience: Home loan and personal lending staff
programs.why: Credit licensees must make reasonable inquiries and assess that credit is not unsuitable, and must keep representatives trained and competent for the credit activities they perform.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 209 Credit licensing: Responsible lending conduct
references.note: ASIC's view of the inquiries, verification and unsuitability assessment required before credit is provided or increased.

references.title: RG 206 Credit licensing: Competence and training
references.provision: NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)
references.note: Credit licensees must keep representatives adequately trained and competent (NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)); ASIC expects initial and ongoing training built into recruitment and supervision.

programs.title: Australia | Internal Dispute Resolution (RG 271)
programs.why: RG 271 sets enforceable standards on complaint timeframes and on staff authority to resolve complaints. ASIC expects induction and ongoing training for complaint staff and IDR awareness for all staff.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 271 Internal dispute resolution
references.note: Sets enforceable IDR standards and expects staff to have authority to resolve complaints; firms should give complaint staff targeted induction and ongoing training and train all staff on the IDR process.
references.provision: RG 271.132(c) and RG 271.150 (training)

programs.title: Australia | Design and Distribution Obligations (RG 274)
programs.why: Issuers and distributors must take reasonable steps so products reach their target market and report significant dealings. ASIC says it will consider whether distributors have given distribution staff sufficient training and assessed their skills.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 274 Product design and distribution obligations
references.note: Issuers and distributors must take reasonable steps so products reach the target market; ASIC will consider whether distribution staff have had sufficient training, including on product attributes and target markets.

programs.title: Australia | Vulnerable Customers under the Banking Code
programs.why: The 2025 Banking Code broadens the meaning of vulnerability and commits banks to train staff to treat vulnerable customers with sensitivity, respect and compassion. It is an industry code binding through contract.

references.title: Banking Code of Practice (2025)
references.provision: Clause 7 (trained and competent staff)
references.note: Industry code binding on subscribing banks; it commits banks to train staff to be competent, to know the Code and to deal with vulnerable customers with care.

references.title: 24-136MR ASIC approves enhanced Banking Code of Practice
references.note: ASIC approval of the 2025 Banking Code of Practice (from 28 February 2025), which broadens financial difficulty, improves accessibility and inclusion, and keeps the diligent and prudent banker standard; ASIC notes the Code binds ABA members through their customer contracts and that ASIC does not enforce it.

programs.title: Australia | Privacy Act 1988 and APP 11 Security of Personal Information
programs.why: APP 11 requires reasonable steps to protect personal information. The OAIC names staff training as an expected step and says it should reach new starters, contractors and temporary staff.

references.title: Privacy Act 1988
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Schedule 1, APP 11.1
references.note: An APP entity must take reasonable steps to protect personal information it holds from misuse, interference, loss and unauthorised access, modification or disclosure; training is not named in the Act.

references.title: Chapter 11: APP 11 Security of personal information
references.provision: Privacy Act 1988, Schedule 1, APP 11
references.note: APP 11 requires reasonable steps to protect personal information; the OAIC lists staff training on privacy and security as an expected organisational step.

references.title: Guide to securing personal information
references.note: OAIC guidance that training should reach new starters, contractors and temporary staff, and that all staff should be able to recognise data breaches.

programs.title: Australia | Debt Collection Conduct (RG 96)
programs.why: The joint ASIC-ACCC guideline sets out acceptable collection conduct under consumer and credit laws. It contains no specific training duty, but collections staff need to know it.

references.title: RG 96 Debt collection guideline: For collectors and creditors
references.note: Joint ASIC-ACCC guidance on acceptable contact, communication and conduct when collecting consumer debts; it suggests creditors and collectors build it into staff training and remain responsible for agents.

programs.title: Australia | Sales Practices and Product Suitability
programs.why: Staff who give advice or arrange financial products or credit must be adequately trained and competent under the licensee duties. DDO obligations add target-market controls on distribution.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 146 Licensing: Training of financial product advisers
references.note: Explains how licensees meet the duty to keep advisers trained and competent; advisers on basic deposit and related non-cash payment products can meet the standard through a course assessed by their licensee.

references.title: RG 206 Credit licensing: Competence and training
references.provision: NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)
references.note: Credit licensees must keep representatives adequately trained and competent (NCCP Act s 47(1)(g)); ASIC expects initial and ongoing training built into recruitment and supervision.

references.title: Regulatory Guide 274 Product design and distribution obligations
references.note: Issuers and distributors must take reasonable steps so products reach the target market; ASIC will consider whether distribution staff have had sufficient training, including on product attributes and target markets.

programs.title: Australia | Information Security Awareness (APRA CPS 234)
programs.why: CPS 234 requires banks to maintain information security capability and controls. APRA's CPG 234 suggests an awareness program for staff, contractors and third parties, tracked and tested at onboarding and periodically.

references.title: Banking: prudential and reporting standards (CPS 234 Information Security)
references.note: Lists CPS 234, in force since 1 July 2019, which requires banks to maintain information security capability commensurate with threats.

references.title: CPG 234 Information Security
references.note: Practice guide to CPS 234 suggesting an information security awareness program for staff, contractors and third parties, tracked and tested at onboarding and periodically.

programs.title: Australia | Phishing and Social Engineering Prevention
programs.why: CPG 234 lists social engineering among recurring awareness topics and suggests reporting phishing test results to the board. This is guidance, not a binding training duty.

references.title: CPG 234 Information Security
references.note: Practice guide to CPS 234 suggesting an information security awareness program for staff, contractors and third parties, tracked and tested at onboarding and periodically.

programs.title: Australia | Notifiable Data Breaches Scheme
programs.why: Eligible data breaches must be assessed and notified to the OAIC and affected individuals. OAIC guidance says all staff should be able to recognise a breach and know how to escalate it.

references.title: Part 1: Data breaches and the Australian Privacy Act
references.note: Explains the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme: eligible breaches must be assessed and notified to affected individuals and the Commissioner.

references.title: Guide to securing personal information
references.note: OAIC guidance that training should reach new starters, contractors and temporary staff, and that all staff should be able to recognise data breaches.

programs.title: Australia | Operational Resilience under APRA CPS 230
programs.why: CPS 230, in force since 1 July 2025 and amended from 1 July 2026, requires banks to manage operational risk and keep critical operations within tolerance. Staff must understand their part in it; no course is prescribed.

references.title: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Requires banks to manage operational risk, maintain critical operations within tolerance through disruptions and manage material service providers; replaced CPS 231 and CPS 232. Amended version in force 1 July 2026.

references.title: Final targeted amendments to CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Limited exemption from contractual requirements for certain non-traditional service providers (e.g. central banks, clearing facilities) from 1 July 2026.

references.title: CPG 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: APRA guidance on implementing CPS 230, including business continuity planning, testing and service provider management.

programs.title: Australia | Material Service Provider Management (CPS 230)
programs.why: CPS 230 replaced CPS 231 on outsourcing. Banks must manage material service providers through policy, due diligence, contracts and monitoring, with narrow exemptions for some providers from 1 July 2026.

references.title: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Requires banks to manage operational risk, maintain critical operations within tolerance through disruptions and manage material service providers; replaced CPS 231 and CPS 232. Amended version in force 1 July 2026.

references.title: Final targeted amendments to CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Limited exemption from contractual requirements for certain non-traditional service providers (e.g. central banks, clearing facilities) from 1 July 2026.

programs.title: Australia | Business Continuity under CPS 230
programs.why: CPS 230 replaced CPS 232 and requires a credible business continuity plan with regular testing. Staff involved need to know their roles; no course is prescribed.

references.title: CPS 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: Requires banks to manage operational risk, maintain critical operations within tolerance through disruptions and manage material service providers; replaced CPS 231 and CPS 232. Amended version in force 1 July 2026.

references.title: CPG 230 Operational Risk Management
references.note: APRA guidance on implementing CPS 230, including business continuity planning, testing and service provider management.

programs.title: Australia | Psychosocial Hazards and Workplace Bullying (WHS)
programs.why: Under the model WHS laws employers must eliminate or minimise psychosocial risks, including bullying and harassment. Safe Work Australia guidance treats training and supervision as support for those controls.

references.title: Psychosocial hazards
references.note: Employers must eliminate or minimise psychosocial risks, including bullying and harassment, so far as reasonably practicable.

references.title: Model Code of Practice: Managing psychosocial hazards at work
references.note: Practical guidance on controls for psychosocial risks, supported by training and supervision.

programs.title: Australia | Sex Discrimination Act Positive Duty
programs.why: Employers must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate sexual harassment, and the Commission can enforce this from 12 December 2023. Its guidelines expect compulsory, ongoing training but the Act does not prescribe it.

references.title: Sex Discrimination Act 1984
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Section 47C (positive duty)
references.note: Employers and PCBUs must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate, as far as possible, unlawful sex discrimination, sexual harassment, sex-based harassment, hostile workplace environments and related victimisation; training is not named in the Act.

references.title: Guidelines for Complying with the Positive Duty under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth)
references.provision: Sex Discrimination Act 1984 s 47C
references.note: Employers must take reasonable and proportionate measures to eliminate sexual harassment; the Commission expects compulsory, ongoing, expert-led training, with more for leaders.

references.title: A Quick Guide for Complying with the Positive Duty under the Sex Discrimination Act 1984
references.note: Summarises the seven standards; training records and content are examples of compliance evidence. Enforcement powers from 12 December 2023.

programs.title: Australia | Work Health and Safety Duties
programs.why: The primary WHS duty requires employers to provide the information, training, instruction or supervision needed to protect workers from health and safety risks. State and territory laws apply this; Victoria has its own OHS Act.

references.title: Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (Cth)
references.issuer: Parliament of Australia (Federal Register of Legislation)
references.provision: Section 19(3)(f)
references.note: The primary duty of care includes ensuring, so far as reasonably practicable, the information, training, instruction or supervision needed to protect all persons from work health and safety risks. States and territories have mirror laws; Victoria has its own OHS Act.

references.title: Guide to the Work Health and Safety Act
references.provision: Model WHS Act s 19 (primary duty of care)
references.note: Explains the primary duty of care in the model WHS Act, which includes providing the information, training, instruction or supervision needed to protect workers.

notes: AML/CTF reform: the AML/CTF Amendment Act 2024 and the AML/CTF Rules 2025 (which replaced the 2007 Rules) applied to existing reporting entities such as banks from 31 March 2026; newly regulated professions followed on 1 July 2026. Personnel due diligence and training now sit in the AML/CTF policies (Act s 26F(4)(d) and (e); Rules ss 5-8 and 5-9), and the policies must also deal with targeted financial sanctions (Rules s 5-3).
AUSTRAC transition: existing reporting entities may keep using the old SMR form and content until 30 March 2029 (Rules s 12-2); the new tipping-off offence began 31 March 2025.
APRA CPS 230 took effect on 1 July 2025, replacing CPS 231 and CPS 232; targeted amendments for certain non-traditional service providers apply from 1 July 2026.
APRA consulted in mid-2026 on a revised CPS 510 that would absorb CPS 520 fit and proper requirements; check whether it has been finalised.

Scams Prevention Framework: banks must join AFCA for SPF purposes by 1 September 2026, and most obligations under the banking code start 31 March 2027; the code was still a draft when consulted on in 2026.

Privacy Act reforms (2024 amending Act): statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy, tiered penalties, automated decision transparency due December 2026, and a Children's Online Privacy Code due by 10 December 2026.
The 2025 Banking Code of Practice took effect on 28 February 2025 with broader vulnerability commitments.
A corporate offence of failing to prevent foreign bribery (Criminal Code s 70.5A) now applies, with an adequate procedures defence and Attorney-General's guidance.
APRA's CPS 230 page shows the guide CPG 230 as superseded on 30 June 2026; entries citing CPG 230 should be re-checked against the current guidance before relying on them.
